analysis.investment_thesis: FirstCry fails both legs of the Magic Formula completely — EBIT is effectively negative (operating margin -0.27% on INR 7,660 Cr revenue) yielding a near-zero or negative Earnings Yield, while ROCE of -0.40% confirms zero return on capital. There is nothing to buy here at any price, let alone at EV/EBITDA of 585x.
key_strengths: Revenue scale and growth: 56.2% CAGR over 7 years, reaching INR 7,660 Cr — genuine category leadership in India's mother-baby segment
Improving EBITDA trajectory: turned positive in FY24 (INR 158 Cr) and expanded to INR 374 Cr in FY25 — directional progress
Gross margin of 35.25% suggests reasonable unit economics before operating cost drag
key_risks: Persistently negative FCF — 0/5 years positive, burning INR 292 Cr in FY25 alone; survival depends on repeated capital raises
Borrowings exploded from INR 34 Cr (FY20) to INR 1,661 Cr (FY25) — finance costs of INR 158 Cr now consume nascent operating profit entirely
Zero promoter holding (0%) removes any alignment incentive and raises governance concerns for a company still losing money
red_flags: EBIT is negative or near-zero — Magic Formula is inapplicable by design
Forward P/E of 785x and EV/EBITDA of 585.5x: market is pricing in a decade of perfect execution for a company with no proven profit
Net losses every year except FY21: cumulative destruction of equity since IPO
Finance cost CAGR of 106% (7Y) — debt servicing growing faster than revenue
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula demands two things: a cheap price (high Earnings Yield = EBIT/EV) and a good business (high ROIC = EBIT / Net Working Capital + Fixed Assets). FirstCry delivers neither. EBIT on an operating basis is roughly -INR 21 Cr (operating margin -0.27% × revenue INR 7,660 Cr), meaning Earnings Yield on an EV of ~INR 14,510 Cr (market cap INR 13,211 Cr + debt INR 1,570 Cr – cash INR 271 Cr) is essentially zero or negative. ROCE of -0.40% and ROE of -4.07% confirm the business has never cleared its cost of capital. The EV/EBITDA of 585x is not a valuation — it is a hope premium.

What makes this worse structurally is the FCF profile: the company has burned cash in every single year of recorded history, with INR 1,299 Cr cumulative FCF destruction from FY20–FY25. Borrowings have compounded at 106% annually over seven years, and finance costs of INR 158 Cr in FY25 now fully offset the INR 158 Cr improvement in EBITDA. The directional improvement in EBITDA (INR -216 Cr in FY23 → INR +374 Cr in FY25) is real and worth noting, but the path to a double-digit Earnings Yield at current market cap is implausible without either a dramatic collapse in the share price or a multi-year earnings inflection. My formula does not reward stories — it rewards numbers.
